newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, Russia move to closer ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan, Russia move to closer ties.

text.p: Japan released $500 million in long-delayed aid to Russia on Friday and Moscow offered the joint development of disputed islands in the biggest steps forward in their ties since the end of the Cold War.

For Russian President Boris Yeltsin the aid resumption was a welcome economic shot in the arm while for Japan the islands proposal took some heat out of similiar rows with China, South Korea and Taiwan.

In the most dramatic gesture of talks in Tokyo between Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and visiting Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, Japan said it was ready to resume disbursing a 1991 aid package consisting of $500 million in Export-Import Bank loans.

The aid package, originally only for "humanitarian assistance" and restricted to medical projects, was frozen in 1991 because of political and economic turmoil in Russia following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"We would like to carry out the $500 million in loans from our Export-Import Bank," Ikeda told Primakov.
Loans could now be available for commercial and industrial projects, the Japanese officials said.

Japanese media reports said possible projects include a car plant outside Moscow, industrial water works at Nahodka in the Russian Far East, and various plants for manufacturing car tyres, baby food and plastic bottles in other parts of Russia.
On its part, Russia formally proposed joint development of islands at the heart of a territorial dispute that has stopped the two countries from signing a World War Two peace treaty.
"We proposed this, not as a subsitution to settle the problem, but as a means to improve overall ties regarding the islands," Primakov told a news conference after the talks.
The islands -- Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai group -- were seized by the Soviet army in the closing days of World War Two.
The volcanic islands, populated by only about 20,000, are northeast of Japan's northernmost island of Hokkaido.

Primakov said possible projects could include fishing, fish canneries and tourism. Waters around the islands, scene of frequent clashes between Japanese fishermen and Russian coastguards, are rich in crab, salmon, and other fish.
Geologists suspect the islands are rich in minerals which have not been developed because of the row.
"We would not hesitate to consider this if Russia makes a detailed proposal," Ikeda told Primakov.
Japan, already locked in islands disputes with South Korea, China and Taiwan, must walk a delicate line on the issue in case there is a knock-on effect.
China also has informally proposed jointly developing oil resources around the Japan-held Senkaku Islands, called Diaoyus and claimed by both China and Taiwan.
For Japan, Russia has always been its traditional enemy, with the two countries fighting two full-scale wars this century and two other undeclared wars before 1945.
"These are two very firm steps taken by the two countries," a Japanese government source said.
After the war, a brief period of rapprochement came in 1956 when Moscow normalised ties with Japan and promised to return two of the disputed islands upon conclusion of a peace treaty.
The two others would be considered after that, it said.
But as the Cold War became more frigid and Japan renewed a military alliance with the United States in 1960, Moscow scrapped the 1956 pledge to giove back two islands,
The thaw leading to Friday's gestures started in 1993 when Yeltsin came to Tokyo and recognised a dispute existed and should be resolved by "law and justice".
